Starting from the standard Transformer architecture (attention layers, feed-forward layers, residual connections, and layer normalization), we identify the two limiting processes involved: (i) a continuous-depth limit ($L $, layer step $ 0$ with $L =T$ fixed), which turns the discrete layer recursion into a coupled system of ordinary differential equations for $n$ tokens on the unit sphere $ S ^ d-1 $ (an interacting particle system); and (ii) a mean-field limit ($n $), which lifts this system to a nonlinear continuity (Vlasov/McKean--Vlasov) equation on the space $ P( S ^ d-1 )$ of probability measures on the sphere, by a stability argument of Dobrushin type together with Sznitman's propagation of chaos. We prove all steps that are elementary---Euler error bounds, Lipschitz estimates for the softmax attention kernel, the Dobrushin stability estimate with explicit constants, existence and uniqueness of measure-valued solutions, and propagation of chaos---and we cite with precise addresses all results that are standard but hard (Kantorovich--Rubinstein duality, completeness of Wasserstein spaces, Picard--Lindel\"of, ojasiewicz's theorem, the center-stable manifold theorem, quantitative empirical-measure rates). We then describe the Wasserstein gradient-flow structure of the limit equation (informally, following Otto calculus), and summarize the known results on its long-time behavior: almost-sure clustering, exponential rates, metastability, and the Kuramoto and mean-shift interpretations. We close with a discussion of stochastic variants and of what is currently rigorous versus heuristic. The only prerequisites assumed are a standard undergraduate background in analysis, linear algebra, and probability. abstract Introduction Transformers and why a limit theory is useful Since their introduction by Vaswani et al.~ vaswani2017attention , Transformers have become the dominant architecture in large-scale machine learning. A Transformer processes an ordered collection $ X=(x_1, ,x_n)$ of $n$ vectors $x_i ^d$, called tokens , by composing a large number $L$ of layers ; each layer mixes two operations, self-attention (through which every token interacts with every other token in a data-dependent way) and a token-wise feed-forward map (MLP) , wrapped in residual connections and normalization maps. Precise definitions of all of these terms are given in Section~ sec:architecture ; for a gentle mathematical introduction to the architecture itself we also refer to Serret~ serret2604 . Because a Transformer is built by iterating near-identical maps, it is natural to ask whether its behavior admits a simpler macroscopic description when the architectural parameters become large. Two parameters are particularly meaningful from a dynamical-systems perspective: enumerate [label=( )] the number $L$ of layers (the depth ); the number $n$ of tokens in the input (the context length ). enumerate The purpose of these notes is to explain---and to prove those parts that are elementary---how these two parameters give rise to the two limiting processes which, composed, define the mean-field limit of a Transformer : quote Depth limit. $L $ with an appropriate rescaling of the per-layer step size turns the discrete layer recursion into a continuous-time system of coupled ordinary differential equations (ODEs) for the $n$ tokens---an interacting particle system . \, Mean-field limit. $n $ lifts this interacting particle system to a deterministic evolution equation for a probability measure on the state space of one token: a nonlinear continuity equation (an equation of Vlasov or McKean--Vlasov type) on $ ( )$. quote This two-step construction, and the models it produces, are due to Geshkovski, Letrouit, Polyanskiy and Rigollet~ geshkovski2025mathematical (building on~ geshkovski2024emergence and on the earlier work~ sander2022sinkformers ); the recent survey of Rigollet~ rigollet2026meanfield develops the long-time behavior of the limiting models (clustering, metastability, connections to synchronization). The depth limit rests on the residual structure of the architecture---the observation that layers with skip connections are time discretizations of a dynamical system goes back to the residual networks of He et al.~ he2016deep,he2016identity and to the Neural-ODE viewpoint~ weinan2017proposal,haber2017stable,chen2018neural . The $n $ step is an instance of the classical mean-field limit of an interacting particle system and its companion notion, propagation of chaos , whose mathematical theory originates in the work of Kac~ kac1956foundations , McKean~ mckean1966class , Braun--Hepp~ braun1977vlasov , Neunzert--Wick~ neunzert1974approximation , Dobrushin~ dobrushin1979vlasov and Sznitman~ sznitman1991topics ; modern accounts are Golse's lecture notes~ golse2016dynamics and the two-part review of Chaintron and Diez~ chaintron2022propagationI, chaintron2022propagationII . These notes are written to be used: for every elementary step we give a proof with all estimates carried out (in particular the Lipschitz analysis of the softmax attention kernel, the Euler error bound for the depth limit, the weak formulation of the continuity equation, the Dobrushin stability estimate with explicit constants, the existence/uniqueness/well-posedness theory for general initial measures, and the proof of propagation of chaos from the stability estimate). Results that are standard but not elementary---the Kantorovich--Rubinstein duality theorem, completeness of the Wasserstein space, the Picard--Lindel\"of theorem, ojasiewicz's convergence theorem, the center-stable manifold theorem, quantitative rates for empirical measures---are stated precisely and cited with exact references (theorem or section numbers) when used.
